passages.t: Jeremiah on trial for his life
passages.happening:
At the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign, God tells Jeremiah to stand in the temple court and speak every word to all who come to worship, holding nothing back (verse 2). ‘Perhaps they will listen and turn’ (verse 3), so that God may relent of the disaster he is planning. If they will not listen and walk in his law and heed his prophets, he will make the temple like Shiloh and the city a curse among the nations (verses 4 to 6).

The priests, the prophets and all the people hear him, and as soon as he finishes they seize him and say he must die (verses 7 and 8). The officials of Judah come up from the palace and sit at the entrance of the New Gate (verse 10). The priests and prophets say the man deserves death for prophesying against the city (verse 11).

Jeremiah answers that the LORD sent him. They must change their ways, and God may relent (verses 12 and 13). ‘As for me, here I am in your hands; do to me what you think is good and right’ (verse 14). But if they kill him, they will bring innocent blood on themselves (verse 15). The officials and the people tell the priests and prophets that he does not deserve death, for he has spoken in the name of the LORD (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The beginning of Jehoiakim's reign points to about 609 or 608 BC. Josiah had just been killed at Megiddo, and Pharaoh Necho had put Jehoiakim on the throne. This is the occasion of the temple sermon of chapter 7, and chapter 26 tells what it cost.

The scene is a trial. The accusers are the priests and prophets. The court is the king's officials, who sit in the gate, the place of judgment. The people swing from accusers to the side of the defense. Jeremiah does not defend himself by softening his message. He repeats it and leaves his life in their hands.

The priests and prophets had the most to lose from a word against the temple. The officials, who served the king, judged the case more fairly than the religious leaders did.
passages.later: Jesus lamented Jerusalem as the city ‘who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her’ (Matthew 23:37). Stephen, on trial before the council, also spoke against trust in the temple (Acts 7:48).
passages.hard:
If God declared disaster and then said he might relent, does he change his mind? Were his warnings real?

The chapter treats God's warnings as real and his relenting as real. Many of the Bible's prophecies of judgment are conditional, even when the condition is not spoken, as Jeremiah 18:7-10 explains: if a nation turns from evil, God will relent of the disaster he planned. Jonah's preaching to Nineveh works the same way. Some theologians stress that God's purpose does not change and that his relenting was always part of it, including the people's response. Others stress that the Bible shows God truly responding to prayer and repentance in time. Both agree that the warnings were meant to be heeded and that a word of judgment is also a call to turn.
passages.asks: Jeremiah put his life in their hands and would not change his message. Ask what you would do if telling the truth put you at risk. And ask whether you hear God's warnings as threats or as invitations to turn.

passages.t: Micah remembered, Uriah killed, Ahikam's protection
passages.happening:
Some of the elders stand up and remind the assembly of Micah of Moresheth, who prophesied in Hezekiah's day that Zion would be plowed like a field and Jerusalem become a heap of rubble (verses 17 and 18). Did Hezekiah put him to death? No, he feared the LORD and sought his favor, and the LORD relented of the disaster. They are about to do great harm to themselves (verse 19).

The chapter then tells of another prophet, Uriah son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim, who prophesied the same things as Jeremiah (verse 20). King Jehoiakim sought to kill him. Uriah fled to Egypt (verse 21). The king sent Elnathan son of Achbor and others after him (verse 22). They brought him back, and Jehoiakim struck him down with the sword and threw his body into the common burial ground (verse 23).

‘Nevertheless, Ahikam son of Shaphan supported Jeremiah, so he was not handed over to the people to be put to death’ (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The elders quote Micah 3:12 almost word for word. This is one of very few places in the Old Testament where an earlier prophet's words are quoted with his name attached, and here they work as a legal precedent. Micah prophesied under Hezekiah, who reigned roughly 715 to 686 BC, and the city was spared because Hezekiah listened.

Uriah's story is set beside Jeremiah's to show how close Jeremiah came to death. The same message, a different outcome. Jehoiakim reached even into Egypt to bring a prophet back to be killed.

Ahikam son of Shaphan came from a family of royal officials who had served Josiah. His son Gedaliah would later be appointed governor and protect Jeremiah again. Faithfulness in one generation shaped the next.
passages.later: The elders quoted Micah: ‘Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble’ (Micah 3:12). Ahikam had been one of Josiah's officials sent to ask about the book of the law (2 Kings 22:12).
passages.asks: Ahikam stood up for Jeremiah when it was dangerous. Ask whom you could stand beside when they are under attack for telling the truth. And ask what precedent from the past could help you see rightly today, as Micah's case helped the elders.
